chunks: What SPI is and stands for. The question: What is SPI? What does it stand for?
SPI stands for Serial Peripheral Interface. It is a way for one chip, the master, to exchange data with another chip, the slave, over four wires.
A shared clock wire sets the pace, so each bit has a clear moment when it counts. The master also uses one wire to pick which slave should listen.
SPI is simple and fast, so flash memory, displays and sensors use it a lot.
Imagine two people sitting across a table, each holding a row of eight cards. A drummer beats a steady rhythm. On every beat, each person slides one card across to the other.
After eight beats, they have traded entire rows. That is SPI: sending and receiving happen on the same beats. The drummer is the clock.
To "read" from the slave, the master hands over throwaway cards and keeps whatever comes back.
MOSI carries the master's register out into the slave's; MISO carries the slave's register back into the master's. SCLK shifts both at the same instant.
CS (active low) selects this slave and frames the transfer.
Master and slave: the master controls the clock and starts every exchange. The slave answers. Newer documents say controller and peripheral.
SCLK: the clock wire, driven by the master. Every tick moves one bit. MOSI and MISO: the data wires. MOSI carries bits from master to slave. MISO carries bits back.
Chip select (CS): a wire the master pulls low to pick one slave and mark the start and end of a transfer. Synchronous: using a shared clock to time each bit.
The master holds one byte, 0xA5, and the slave holds another, 0x3C. ("0x" marks hexadecimal, a short way to write bytes.) The master pulls chip select low.
Then it sends eight clock ticks. On each tick, one bit leaves the master on MOSI while one bit leaves the slave on MISO.
After eight ticks, the master holds 0x3C and the slave holds 0xA5. Then chip select goes high. That is the whole idea.
"SPI is Serial Peripheral Interface: a synchronous, full-duplex bus with one master and one or more slaves, using SCLK, MOSI, MISO and a chip select.
It works as two shift registers in a ring: on each clock the master and slave swap one bit, so after eight clocks they've exchanged a byte.
Push-pull drivers make it fast, but there's no addressing, ACK or formal standard. The master picks the slave with CS and sets the mode (CPOL and CPHA)."
